## 1. Introduction 

Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in higher education, reshaping pedagogical possibilities and raising urgent concerns regarding instructional readiness (Kasneci et al., 2023). Unlike conventional educational technologies that primarily support content presentation and assessment administration, generative AI tools possess the capacity to create original content, simulate dialog, and provide adaptive feedback. In doing so, AI tools fundamentally alter the dynamics of teacher-technology interaction (Crompton & Burke, [2023)](#orcid). Within Chinese higher education, national policies have strongly advocated for AI integration into curricula since 2018. However, the gap between institutional ambitions and actual classroom adoption remains substantial (F. Wang et al., 2023). Understanding the determinants of teachers’ AI use intention in education is therefore a pressing concern for both researchers and policymakers. 

Research on technology adoption in education has primarily relied on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) to explain behavioral intentions (Scherer et al., 2019; Venkatesh et al., 2003). While these frameworks have demonstrated robust explanatory power for general-purpose technologies, they offer limited insight into the domain-specific knowledge structures. Such knowledge structures are needed for meaningfully embedding novel tools into disciplinary instruction (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). The Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework addresses this limitation by conceptualizing effective technology integration as an interplay among content expertise, pedagogical strategies, and technological competence (Koehler & Mishra, 2009). Recent studies have extended this framework to accommodate AI-specific competencies, yielding the construct of AI-TPACK (An et al., [2026;](#orcid) Celik, [2023)](#orcid). Empirical work has established that TPACK-related constructs are associated with technology adoption intentions among higher education teachers (AI-Adwan et al., [2024;](#orcid) Ma & Lei,

2024; Sun et al., 2024). Teachers with stronger AI-TPACK may therefore be better positioned to use AI effectively in instruction. However, it remains insufficiently explained how this form of professional knowl- edge is translated into AI use intention through psychological mechanisms. 

A growing body of research in educational technology has identified self-efficacy as a key psychological mechanism linking teachers’ knowledge and competence to their technology adoption intentions. Studies have shown that self-efficacy mediates the relationship between TPACK and behavioral intentions (Joo et al., 2018; Scherer et al., 2019). This suggests that the influence of knowledge on adoption is partly channeled through individuals’ confidence in their own capabilities. However, whether AI self-efficacy specifically medi- ates the relationship between AI-TPACK and AI use intention among university teachers remains underexam- ined. Existing studies have tended to treat AI self-efficacy either as an independent predictor or as an outcome of AI-related knowledge, rather than as a mediating mechanism within an integrated model (H. Du et al., [2026;](#orcid) Y. Y. Wang & Chuang, 2024). Accordingly, the present study conceptualizes AI self-efficacy as teachers’ confidence in effectively integrating AI tools into instructional contexts and examines its mediating role between AI-TPACK and AI use intention. 

Beyond this indirect process, the strength of the relationship may also depend on important boundary conditions. A potentially critical moderator is AI dependence, which captures individuals’ excessive reliance on AI tools across emotional, functional, cognitive, and behavioral dimensions (Wu et al., 2025). Although moderate engagement with AI can build competence and confidence, excessive dependence may weaken the extent to which knowledge is translated into robust self-efficacy and subsequent AI use intention. Specifically, teachers overly reliant on AI might develop a fragile sense of efficacy that depends more on tool availability than on authentic pedagogical mastery (Y. Du et al., [2026;](#orcid) Šerić & Praničević, 2026). While AI dependence has attracted increasing attention in educational research, its moderating influence on this self-efficacy-mediated pathway from AI-TPACK to AI use intention remains empirically unexplored. 

Furthermore, the disciplinary background may also shape teachers’ AI-related perceptions and behav- iors. Generative AI tools offer differentiated affordances across academic domains, and their integration inherently varies by field. For instance, generative AI may support data analysis and hypothesis generation in the natural sciences, while in the social sciences it may facilitate literature synthesis and qualitative coding. Similarly, AI tools may assist with lesson planning and differentiated instruction in education, whereas in the arts they may raise distinctive concerns regarding creativity and authenticity (Andersen et al., [2025;](#orcid) Celik et al., [2025;](#orcid) Millet et al., 2023; Than et al., 2025). Empirical evidence underscores the signifi- cance of these domain-specific variations, revealing substantial disparities in the breadth and intensity of AI adoption across higher education disciplines (Mohammadi et al., 2026). Correspondingly, teacher- focused research identifies disciplinary background as a critical determinant in the development of university teachers’ AI literacy and related digital competencies (Starkey et al., 2023). As disciplinary con- text can shape teachers’ AI-related knowledge, confidence, and reliance (Mah & Groß, 2024; Shata & Hart- ley, 2025), it is necessary to examine whether these variables differ significantly across academic disciplines. 

To address these identified gaps, the present study is guided by four specific research questions: 

RQ1. Is AI-TPACK significantly associated with AI use intention? 

RQ2. Does AI self-efficacy mediate the relationship between AI-TPACK and AI use intention? 

RQ3. Does AI dependence moderate the direct and indirect relationships among AI-TPACK, AI self-efficacy, and AI use intention? 

RQ4. Are there significant disciplinary differences in AI-TPACK, AI self-efficacy, AI use intention, and AI dependence? 

By integrating AI-TPACK, AI self-efficacy, AI dependence, and disciplinary background within one moderated mediation model, this study extends prior teacher technology adoption research from direct-effect explana- tions toward a conditional psychological process account of AI use intention.

## 2. Theoretical foundation and hypotheses 

### _2.1._ _Theoretical foundation_ 

#### _2.1.1._ _Social cognitive theory_ 

Social Cognitive Theory (SCT), developed by Bandura ([1986)](#orcid), provides the theoretical framework for this study. SCT posits a triadic reciprocal relationship among personal, behavioral, and environmental factors in explaining human functioning. Within this framework, self-efficacy refers to individuals’ beliefs in their capa- bility to organize and execute the courses of action required to manage prospective situations. Conse- quently, self-efficacy influences the choices individuals make, the effort they expend, their persistence in the face of obstacles, and ultimately their performance outcomes (Bandura, [1997)](#orcid). 

In the context of AI integration in education, SCT offers a clear explanatory logic for the pathway from knowledge to intention. Stronger AI-TPACK can provide the cognitive foundation upon which teachers’ competence beliefs are built (H. Du et al., [2026)](#orcid). Through applying their knowledge in practice, teachers accumulate mastery experiences, which Bandura identified as the most potent source of self-efficacy. These experiences, in turn, strengthen their behavioral intentions toward AI use (Y. Wang et al., 2021). SCT thus sup- ports a sequential pathway in which AI-TPACK fosters AI self-efficacy, which subsequently strengthens AI use intention in education. 

SCT also provides a basis for identifying boundary conditions that shape this pathway. Bandura ([1997)](#orcid) emphasized that self-efficacy beliefs are most effectively cultivated through effortful, reflective engagement with challenging tasks. When contextual or behavioral factors undermine autonomous cognitive func- tioning, the translation of knowledge into self-efficacy and subsequent intentions may be attenuated. In the present study, AI dependence represents one such constraining condition, as excessive reliance on AI tools may reduce the reflective engagement required for the development of robust self-efficacy beliefs. 

#### _2.1.2._ _The TPACK framework in the AI era_ 

The TPACK framework, originally proposed by Mishra and Koehler (2006), conceptualizes effective technology- enhanced teaching as the intersection of three core knowledge domains: technological knowledge, pedagogical knowledge, and content knowledge. Technological knowledge refers to teachers’ understanding of educational technologies, pedagogical knowledge concerns teaching methods and learning design, and content knowledge refers to teachers’ understanding of the subject matter they teach. The value of TPACK lies in its emphasis on the integration of these domains rather than their separate possession. From this perspective, teachers with stronger TPACK are better able to make situated decisions about when, why, and in what ways a technology should be used to support learning, instead of simply adding digital tools to existing teaching routines (Chai et al., [2013; ](#orcid)Koehler & Mishra, 2009; Voogt et al., 2013). This framework has guided extensive research on how teachers develop integrated knowledge for meaningful technology use in education. 

The emergence of AI as an educational technology has necessitated an expansion of the technological knowledge component within TPACK. Unlike conventional technologies that function as passive tools, AI sys- tems exhibit agency-like characteristics, including autonomous decision-making, content generation, and adaptive responsiveness (Guggemos & Seufert, [2021;](#orcid) Holmes et al., 2019; Luckin & Holmes, 2016). These characteristics require teachers to extend their technological knowledge beyond operational familiarity. In AI-supported teaching, teachers therefore need to evaluate the reliability and instructional relevance of AI- generated outputs and consider how adaptive feedback or recommendations should be used pedagogically (Celik, [2023;](#orcid) Crompton & Burke, [2023)](#orcid). They must also address ethical concerns in AI-based decisions, includ- ing the risk of overreliance on AI tools (Chiu et al., [2025;](#orcid) Zhai et al., 2024). AI integration therefore expands TPACK from knowledge of technology use toward professional judgment about AI-supported teaching. 

In the present study, AI-TPACK refers to teachers’ integrated professional knowledge for selecting, evalu- ating, and using AI-based tools in ways that are aligned with disciplinary content, instructional goals, student learning needs, and ethical principles. This construct extends conventional TPACK by making the distinctive affordances and risks of AI explicit within teachers’ pedagogical and content-related decision-making. More specifically, AI-TPACK involves interactional knowledge of AI tools, pedagogical knowledge of AI affordances, content-specific knowledge of field-related AI applications, integrated knowledge for designing AI- supported teaching strategies, and ethical knowledge for evaluating AI use in education (Celik, [2023)](#orcid). This 

4 H. WU ET AL. 

definition avoids treating AI-TPACK as general digital competence. It also distinguishes AI-TPACK from broader AI-competence frameworks. Such frameworks commonly emphasize AI knowledge, application, evaluation, ethical awareness, and human-centered orientations, whereas AI-TPACK situates these compe- tencies within teachers’ instructional design, subject teaching, and classroom decision-making (Chiu et al., [2025)](#orcid). 

This teacher-specific interpretation is also consistent with recent attempts to refine AI-related teaching knowledge. Celik ([2023)](#orcid) introduced the concept of Intelligent-TPACK, arguing that AI integration requires not only technical understanding but also ethical competence in evaluating AI-based decisions. Chiu et al. ([2025)](#orcid) subsequently elaborated AI-specific teaching competencies spanning from AI knowledge to human- centered education, while An et al. ([2026)](#orcid) developed a refined model distinguishing between knowledge required by human teachers and knowledge applicable to AI as a machine teacher. Collectively, these studies suggest that AI integration requires a more specialized and expanded knowledge base than conventional educational technology integration. They provide the conceptual basis for treating AI-TPACK as the central predictor in the present study because it captures the teacher knowledge most directly connected to AI- supported instructional decision-making. 

Taken together, SCT and the AI-TPACK perspective provide an integrated basis for explaining how AI- related professional knowledge may influence AI use intention through self-efficacy, while also accounting for variation in this process across different levels of AI dependence. 

### _2.2._ _Hypothesis development_ 

#### _2.2.1._ _AI-TPACK and AI use intention_ 

TPACK-related constructs have been consistently linked to technology adoption intentions within educa- tional research. For instance, Sun et al. (2024) found that pre-service STEM teachers’ TPACK was significantly associated with their willingness to integrate AI. Ma and Lei (2024) reported similar findings among teacher education students in China. The theoretical rationale underpinning this relationship is straightforward: teachers who possess integrated knowledge about how AI intersects with pedagogy and content are better equipped to envision practical applications, which may increase their readiness and intention to adopt AI tools (Ertmer & Ottenbreit-Leftwich, [2010;](#orcid) Joo et al., 2018). Extending this established logic to the domain of AI, it is reasonable to expect that teachers’ AI-TPACK will similarly demonstrate a significant positive relation- ship with their AI use intention. When teachers deeply understand how to integrate AI capabilities into their specific disciplinary teaching, their behavioral intention to adopt these tools naturally strengthens (Sun et al., 2024; Yurt & Kaşarcı, 2025). Based on the foregoing analysis, the following hypothesis was proposed: 

H1: AI-TPACK is significantly and positively associated with AI use intention. 

#### _2.2.2._ _The mediating role of AI self-efficacy_ 

According to SCT, knowledge resources constitute a foundation upon which self-efficacy beliefs are con- structed (Bandura, [1997)](#orcid). When teachers possess strong AI-TPACK, they have the cognitive basis for envi- sioning successful AI integration, a process that may strengthen their confidence in executing AI-enhanced teaching activities. H. Du et al. ([2026)](#orcid) demonstrated that AI-TPACK was significantly associated with teachers’ self-efficacy in using AI to engage students. Similarly, Dong et al. ([2020)](#orcid) found that TPACK was positively linked to computer self-efficacy among teachers. These findings suggest that AI-TPACK may positively pre- dict AI self-efficacy. 

Higher self-efficacy may translate into stronger behavioral intentions as confident teachers perceive lower barriers and greater expected returns from integration efforts (Bandura, [1997)](#orcid). Wang and Chuang (2024) showed that AI self-efficacy was positively correlated with motivated learning behaviors and technology- related intentions. In the educational technology literature, self-efficacy has been consistently identified as a predictor of technology integration behavior (Scherer et al., 2019). These findings suggest that higher AI self- efficacy may be associated with stronger AI use intention. 

Taken together, these arguments indicate that AI-TPACK may influence AI use intention not only directly but also indirectly through AI self-efficacy. Joo et al. (2018) provided direct evidence for such a mediated 

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 5 

relationship, finding that self-efficacy mediated the association between TPACK and technology use inten- tion among pre-service teachers. Accordingly, the following hypotheses were proposed: 

H2: AI-TPACK is significantly and positively associated with AI self-efficacy. 

H3: AI self-efficacy is significantly and positively associated with AI use intention. 

H4: AI self-efficacy mediates the association between AI-TPACK and AI use intention. 

#### _2.2.3._ _The moderating role of AI dependence_ 

AI dependence, conceptualized as an excessive reliance on AI tools manifesting across emotional, functional, cognitive, and behavioral dimensions (Wu et al., 2025), represents a critical boundary condition in the pro- posed model. The cognitive dependence dimension is particularly relevant, as it involves the systematic offloading of higher-order thinking to AI, thereby eroding independent problem-solving capabilities (Zhai et al., 2024). 

From the perspective of SCT, self-efficacy is most effectively built through effortful mastery experiences that require active and reflective engagement (Bandura, [1997)](#orcid). When teachers are overly dependent on AI, their knowledge application may become passive and superficial. Rather than developing confidence through reflective practice informed by AI-TPACK, dependent teachers may develop a fragile form of efficacy that is contingent on AI availability rather than grounded in authentic competence. This pattern is consistent with the paradox of self-efficacy and technological dependence identified by Zhang and Xu (2025). In addi- tion, Wu et al. (2025) found that AI dependence was negatively associated with academic self-efficacy, pro- viding direct support for this weakening effect. Drawing upon this theoretical rationale, the following hypothesis is proposed: 

H5: AI dependence moderates the association between AI-TPACK and AI self-efficacy. 

Beyond the mediated pathway, AI dependence may also moderate the direct association between AI-TPACK and AI use intention. For highly dependent teachers, AI-TPACK may not translate effectively into intentional adoption because their engagement patterns are driven by compulsive reliance rather than by purposeful pedagogical reasoning (Y. Du et al., [2026)](#orcid). The knowledge-to-intention link requires reflective evaluation of how AI capabilities align with instructional goals, a process that dependence may disrupt (An et al., [2026;](#orcid) Celik, [2023)](#orcid). Accordingly, we advance the following hypothesis: 

H6: AI dependence moderates the direct association between AI-TPACK and AI use intention.

## 3. Method 

### _3.1._ _Participants and sampling_ 

The study was conducted at a normal university in southwestern China, which employed 1381 full-time teachers. Teachers were eligible to participate if they were employed by the university during the data collection period, had experience with university teaching, and voluntarily provided informed consent. Based on this population, the minimum required sample size was 302, according to the guidelines by Krejcie and Morgan (1970). To account for the potential impact of disciplinary backgrounds on AI-related constructs, stratified random sampling was employed. Participants were divided into four disciplinary groups, and were randomly selected from each group in proportions matching the university’s demographic structure. 

Considering potential non-responses and invalid data, 450 online surveys were distributed via the Wen- juanxing platform. During data screening, responses with abnormally short completion times, extensive missing values, or patterned answers were excluded. As a result, 407 valid questionnaires were retained, representing an effective response rate of 90.4%. 

[Table 1 ](#3-method)presents the demographic details of the final sample. The participants included 56.3% males and 43.7% females. The majority were mid-career and senior educators, with 69.5% aged between 30 and 50, and 74.0% having over 10 years of teaching experience. In terms of highest degree, 50.9% held a bachelor’s degree, 37.3% a master’s degree, and 11.8% a doctorate. Disciplinary backgrounds included Social Sciences (49.9%), Education (31.7%), Natural Sciences (13.3%), and the Arts (5.2%). Notably, 72.1% of the participants reported using AI tools at least once a week, demonstrating relatively active engagement with AI. 

The study protocol received approval from the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the researchers’ univer- sity. All participants were provided with a detailed information sheet and gave written informed consent prior to participation. The data collection process was voluntary and anonymous. Participants were fully informed of the study’s purpose, the exclusive use of their data for research, and their right to withdraw at any time without penalty. The general study purpose was provided as part of the informed-consent process so that participants could understand the scope of the research before deciding whether to participate. However, the information sheet did not present the proposed model or disclose the hypothesized relation- ships among AI-TPACK, AI self-efficacy, AI dependence, and AI use intention. Participants were also informed that there were no right or wrong answers and that their responses would not be used for institutional eval- uation. All procedures were conducted in accordance with the ethical standards stipulated in the Declaration of Helsinki.

### _3.2._ _Measures_ 

#### _3.2.1._ _AI-TPACK_ 

AI-TPACK was measured using the 27-item Intelligent-TPACK scale developed by Celik ([2023)](#orcid). This scale was specifically designed to capture teachers’ professional knowledge for integrating AI-based tools into educa- tion, extending the TPACK framework to address both pedagogical and AI-related dimensions of AI use. This scale was selected because it operationalizes AI-TPACK as teacher-specific knowledge for AI-supported instruction, thereby aligning the measurement with the conceptual focus of the present study rather than treating the construct as general digital competence, general AI literacy, or broad technology acceptance. 

It comprises five sub-dimensions: Intelligent-TK (5 items), which captures knowledge to interact with and use AI-based tools; Intelligent-TPK (7 items), which addresses the knowledge of the pedagogical affordances of AI tools, such as personalized feedback and student monitoring; Intelligent-TCK (4 items), which focuses on knowledge of field-specific AI tools; Intelligent-TPACK (7 items), which measures integrated knowledge to select and use suitable AI tools for performing teaching strategies in a particular domain; and Ethics (ET, 4 items). Sample items include “I know how to interact with AI-based tools in daily life” (TK), “I can evaluate the usefulness of feedback from AI-based tools for teaching and learning” (TPK), “I am aware of various AI-based tools which are used by professionals in my teaching field” (TCK), and “In teaching my field, I know how to use different AI-based tools for personalized learning” (TPACK). Items originally developed in the Turkish educational context were carefully adapted for the Chinese university teaching context. These adaptations were reviewed by two educational technology experts for contextual appropriateness and piloted with 52 non-participating teachers from the same university prior to formal data collection. All items were rated on a 7-point Likert scale from 1 (“strongly disagree”) to 7 (“strongly agree”), with higher scores indicating higher levels of AI-TPACK. The original study reported Cronbach’s alpha values of 0.856 for TK, 0.858 for TPK, 0.868 for TCK, 0.895 for TPACK, and 0.864 for ET (Celik, [2023)](#orcid). 

In this study, CFA indicated acceptable construct validity for the five-factor structure, with chi-squared/df = 1.231, CFI = 0.984, TLI = 0.982, and RMSEA = 0.024. The overall Cronbach’s alpha was 0.935. The five dimen- sions showed satisfactory reliabilities: alpha = 0.828 (TK), 0.861 (TPK), 0.833 (TCK), 0.866 (TPACK), and 0.787 (ET). 

#### _3.2.2._ _AI self-efficacy_ 

AI self-efficacy was assessed using the AI Self-Efficacy Scale (AISES) developed by Wang and Chuang (2024). In the present study, this construct is interpreted as teachers’ perceived confidence and comfort in engag- ing with AI in education. This operationalization is conceptually aligned with SCT’s emphasis on efficacy- related confidence, while also reflecting the interactional characteristics captured by the adopted scale. The AISES comprises 22 items across four dimensions: assistance (AS, 7 items), anthropomorphic interaction (AI, 5 items), comfort with AI (CF, 6 items), and technological skills (TS, 4 items). Example items include “I find that AI technologies/products are helpful for learning” (AS), “I think the interactive process of AI technologies/products is very vivid, just like chatting with a real person” (AI), “When interacting with AI technologies/products, I feel very relaxed” (CF), and “AI technologies/products jargon does not baffle me” (TS). All items were rated on a 7-point Likert scale from 1 (“strongly disagree”) to 7 (“strongly agree”), with higher scores reflecting stronger perceived confidence in AI engagement. In the original validation, the overall Cronbach’s alpha was 0.96 (Y. Y. Wang & Chuang, 2024). 

In the current study, CFA supported the four-factor structure, with chi-squared/df = 1.312, CFI = 0.984, TLI = 0.981, and RMSEA = 0.028. The overall Cronbach’s alpha was 0.938. Dimension-level alpha values were 0.855 (AS), 0.835 (AI), 0.845 (CF), and 0.780 (TS). 

#### _3.2.3._ _AI use intention_ 

AI use intention in education was measured using the five-item Behavioral Intention Scale adapted from Yurt and Kaşarcı (2025). In this study, AI use intention refers not only to teachers’ intention to directly integrate AI into classroom teaching, but also to their intention to continue learning about, following, and engaging with AI for teaching-related professional purposes. Accordingly, the construct captures both direct instructional integration intention and broader teaching-related professional engagement with AI. Items include “I will continue to learn about AI knowledge for my professional teaching life,” “I will keep myself updated with the 

8 H. WU ET AL. 

latest AI applications for my professional development,” “I plan to spend time in learning AI technology in the future to enhance my teaching quality,” “I will pay more attention to emerging AI applications for my profes- sional development,” and “I intend to use AI to assist my teaching.” All items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale, with higher scores indicating stronger teaching-related AI use intention. Original validation reported alpha = 0.93 (Yurt & Kaşarcı, 2025). 

In this study, CFA showed good validity: chi-squared/df = 2.730, CFI = 0.989, TLI = 0.979, RMSEA = 0.065. Cronbach’s alpha was 0.857. 

#### _3.2.4._ _AI dependence_ 

AI dependence was assessed using the AI Dependence Scale developed by Wu et al. (2025). This 22-item scale captures maladaptive overreliance on AI across four dimensions: emotional dependence (ED, 5 items), functional dependence (FD, 6 items), cognitive dependence (CD, 5 items), and loss of control (LC, 6 items). Example items include “I feel uneasy or insecure without the help of AI” (ED), “I delegate almost all my aca- demic tasks to AI because it performs them faster and better than I do” (FD), “I often ask AI for answers directly without thinking for myself first” (CD), and “I have tried to reduce my use of AI, but I have never suc- ceeded for long” (LC). All items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale, with higher scores reflecting higher levels of AI dependence. Original validation reported alpha = 0.87 (Wu et al., 2025). 

Although the AIDep-22 was originally validated among Chinese undergraduates, its core dimensions were considered conceptually transferable to teachers’ AI use. Minor wording adjustments were made where necessary to fit the teaching context, and the CFA results in the present sample supported the adequacy of this adaptation. CFA showed chi-squared/df = 1.119, CFI = 0.994, TLI = 0.994, RMSEA = 0.017. The overall alpha was 0.938. Dimension-level values were 0.850 (ED), 0.869 (FD), 0.869 (CD), and 0.870 (LC). 

#### _3.2.5._ _Control variables_ 

In line with research on teachers’ technology adoption (Scherer et al., 2019; Yusuf et al., 2024), demographic and usage-related characteristics that may influence teachers’ AI-related experiences and competencies were controlled for in the statistical models. The control variables included gender, age, educational back- ground, teaching experience, AI use frequency, and disciplinary background. 

### _3.3._ _Data analysis_ 

Data analysis was performed using SPSS 27.0, Amos 27.0, and the PROCESS macro (Hayes, 2017). To preserve the psychometric integrity and validated properties of the instruments, their original response formats were retained. Before the main analyses, data screening was conducted to examine missing values, invalid response patterns, and the distributional properties of the main variables. Univariate normality was assessed using skewness and kurtosis values. The analytical procedure consisted of four systematic steps. 

First, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and reliability analyses were conducted for each instrument. Subsequently, an overall four-construct measurement model was evaluated to confirm discriminant validity. Second, given that all data were self-reported, common method bias (CMB) was rigorously examined. Harman’s single-factor test was used as a preliminary diagnostic, while the unmeasured Common Latent Fac- tor (CLF) approach was employed as the primary and more robust assessment (Podsakoff et al., 2012). Third, descriptive statistics, normality indices, and Pearson correlations were computed to summarize the central tendencies, distributional characteristics, and bivariate relationships among the main variables. 

Finally, hypothesis testing was conducted in two main phases. The PROCESS macro (Model 4) was first uti- lized to test the direct and indirect effects linking AI-TPACK, AI self-efficacy, and AI use intention (H1-H4). Model 8 was then applied to examine the moderated mediation, specifically whether AI dependence moder- ates the pathways from AI-TPACK to both AI self-efficacy and AI use intention (H5, H6). For these analyses, the bootstrap method with 5000 resamples was used to generate 95% bias-corrected Confidence Interval (CI), with effects considered significant if the intervals excluded zero. Additionally, disciplinary differences were examined using one-way ANOVA. When the assumption of homogeneity of variance was violated, Welch’s test and Games-Howell post hoc comparisons were employed.

## 4. Results 

### _4.1._ _Measurement model evaluation_ 

The overall four-construct measurement model was evaluated using CFA. The model demonstrated good fit: chi-squared/df = 1.12, CFI = 0.976, TLI = 0.975 and RMSEA = 0.017. Alternative models showed poorer fit, including a three-factor model (chi-squared/df = 1.31, CFI = 0.939, TLI = 0.937, RMSEA = 0.028), a two-factor model (chi-squared/df = 1.57, CFI = 0.889, TLI = 0.885, RMSEA = 0.037), and a single-factor model (chi- squared/df = 1.73, CFI = 0.856, TLI = 0.852, RMSEA = 0.042). These results support the superiority of the hypothesized four-construct measurement model over the alternative models. As shown in [Table 2,](#4-results) the measurement model also demonstrated good convergent validity and discriminant validity. Overall, these results indicate that the four constructs were measured reliably and distinctly, providing a solid measure- ment foundation for the subsequent analyses. 

### _4.2._ _Common method bias test_ 

To assess the potential threat of CMB, Harman’s single-factor test and the CLF approach were employed. The unrotated principal component analysis showed that 13 factors with eigenvalues greater than 1 were extracted, and the first factor accounted for 20.787% of the total variance, which was below the recom- mended threshold of 40%, indicating that no single factor accounted for most of the covariance among the measures. In addition, the comparison of the CFA models with and without CLF showed no significant change in overall model fit after the inclusion of the latent common method factor. Taken together, these results suggest that the present data were unlikely to be substantially affected by CMB. 

### _4.3._ _Descriptive statistics and correlation analysis_ 

[Table 3 ](#4-results)presents the descriptive statistics and Pearson correlation coefficients for the key variables. Partici- pants reported relatively high levels of AI-TPACK (_M_ = 4.32, SD = 1.12) and AI self-efficacy (_M_ = 4.38, SD = 0.99), a moderate level of AI use intention (_M_ = 3.57, SD = 0.85), and a comparatively lower level of AI depen- dence (_M_ = 2.92, SD = 0.79). The skewness values ranged from −0.446 to −0.004, and the kurtosis values ranged from −0.495 to −0.225. These values indicated no severe departure from univariate normality among the main variables. The correlation analysis showed that AI-TPACK was positively associated with AI self- efficacy (_r_ = 0.455, _p_ \< .001) and AI use intention (_r_ = 0.407, _p_ \< .001), but was not significantly related to AI dependence (_r_ = −0.094, _p_ = .058). AI self-efficacy was positively correlated with AI use intention (_r_ = 0.422, _p_ \< .001) and negatively correlated with AI dependence (_r_ = −0.193, _p_ \< .001), whereas the association between AI use intention and AI dependence was not significant (_r_ = 0.035, _p_ = .481).

### _4.4._ _The mediating role of AI self-efficacy_ 

Model 4 of the PROCESS macro in SPSS was used to examine the mediating role of AI self-efficacy in the rela- tionship between AI-TPACK and AI use intention, while controlling for gender, age, discipline, degree, teach- ing experience, and AI use frequency. Before presenting the statistical estimates, a methodological note regarding the reporting of coefficients is warranted. Given that the focal constructs were measured using scales with varying original scoring formats, standardized coefficients (_β_) are reported for the primary media- tion model ([Table 4)](#44-the-mediating-role-of-ai-self-efficacy) to facilitate a direct and meaningful comparison of effect sizes across variables. Con- versely, unstandardized coefficients (b) are exclusively reported for all subsequent analyses, including the bootstrap estimates of indirect effects ([Table 5)](#44-the-mediating-role-of-ai-self-efficacy) and the moderated mediation models (Tables [6 ](#45-the-moderating-role-of-ai-dependence)and [7)](#45-the-moderating-role-of-ai-dependence). This analytical choice aligns with established statistical guidelines (Hayes, 2017), as unstandardized metrics are mathematically strictly required for the accurate computation of bootstrap CIs and the valid interpretation of interaction terms. 

As shown in [Table 4,](#44-the-mediating-role-of-ai-self-efficacy) AI-TPACK had a significant positive total effect on AI use intention, with a moderate effect (_β_ = .39, _p_ \< .001). In the mediation model, AI-TPACK also significantly and positively predicted AI self- efficacy (_β_ = .40, _p_ \< .001). When AI-TPACK and AI self-efficacy were entered simultaneously into the full model, AI self-efficacy remained a significant positive predictor of AI use intention (_β_ = .29, _p_ \< .001), and the direct effect of AI-TPACK remained significant but was reduced (_β_ = .27, _p_ \< .001). This pattern indicates that AI self-efficacy partially mediated the relationship between AI-TPACK and AI use intention. Accordingly, hypotheses H1, H2, and H3 were supported. [Figure 2 ](#45-the-moderating-role-of-ai-dependence)illustrates the regression paths and corresponding coefficients among the variables. 

The bootstrap results in [Table 5 ](#44-the-mediating-role-of-ai-self-efficacy)further supported this conclusion. Specifically, the total effect of AI-TPACK on AI use intention was 0.293 (SE = 0.037, 95% CI \[0.220, 0.366\]), the direct effect was 0.206 (SE = 0.039, 95% CI \[0.131, 0.282\]), and the indirect effect through AI self-efficacy was 0.087 (BootSE = 0.018, 95% CI \[0.054, 0.126\]). As the CI for the indirect effect did not include zero, the mediation effect was statistically significant. Thus, hypothesis H4 was supported. The indirect pathway accounted for 29.60% of the total effect.

### _4.5._ _The moderating role of AI dependence_ 

Model 8 of the PROCESS macro in SPSS was employed to examine whether AI dependence moderated the direct path from AI-TPACK to AI use intention and the indirect path through AI self-efficacy, while controlling for gender, age, discipline, degree, teaching experience, and AI use frequency. 

[Table 6 ](#45-the-moderating-role-of-ai-dependence)shows that the interaction between AI-TPACK and AI dependence significantly and negatively pre- dicted both AI self-efficacy (_b_ = −0.10, _p_ = .027) and AI use intention (_b_ = −0.08, _p_ = .033). This indicates that AI dependence played a moderating role in both the first-stage path from AI-TPACK to AI self-efficacy and the direct path from AI-TPACK to AI use intention. Therefore, H5 and H6 were both supported. 

### Further simple slope analyses were conducted to clarify these moderation effects (see [Figure 3)](#46-disciplinary-differences), and the results were consistent with the conditional indirect effects reported in [Table 7. ](#45-the-moderating-role-of-ai-dependence)For AI self-efficacy, the posi- tive effect of AI-TPACK was significant at low (_b_ = 0.421, _p_ \< .001), mean (_b_ = 0.340, _p_ \< .001), and high (_b_ =

A similar pattern was found for AI use intention, with the direct effect of AI-TPACK decreasing from 0.278 at low AI dependence to 0.211 at the mean level, and further down to 0.144 at high AI dependence, although all remained significant. In addition, [Table 7 ](#45-the-moderating-role-of-ai-dependence)shows that the indirect effect of AI-TPACK on AI use intention through AI self-efficacy was significant at all three levels of AI dependence and declined as AI dependence increased. The index of moderated mediation was also significant (Index = −0.027, 95% CI \[−0.054, −0.003\]). Collectively, these findings suggest that higher AI dependence weakened both the direct and indirect positive effects of AI-TPACK on AI use intention. 

### _4.6._ _Disciplinary differences_ 

Finally, differences across discipline groups were examined. As shown in [Table 8,](#46-disciplinary-differences) Levene’s test indicated that the assumption of homogeneity of variance was met for AI-TPACK and AISE (_p_ \> .05), but was violated for AIUI and AID (_p_ \< .05). Accordingly, Welch’s test was additionally consulted for the two variables with unequal variances. The Welch results showed that the group difference remained significant for AIUI (Welch’s F (3, 76.67) = 7.01, _p_ \< .001), whereas no significant difference was found for AID (Welch’s F (3, 74.75) = 0.27, _p_ = . 844); therefore, only the significant outcome was interpreted further. Given these differences in variance homogeneity across variables, Games-Howell post hoc comparisons were used to provide a more robust basis for group comparisons. 

As presented in [Table 8,](#46-disciplinary-differences) significant discipline-based differences were found for AI-TPACK, F (3, 403) = 25.93, _p_ \< .001, ηp2 = .162, AISE, F (3, 403) = 15.11, _p_ \< .001, ηp2 = .101, and AIUI, F (3, 403) = 6.29, _p_ \< .001, ηp2 = .045, whereas AID did not differ significantly across disciplines, F (3, 403) = 0.36, _p_ = .786, ηp2 = .003. The effect sizes suggest a comparatively strong disciplinary effect for AI-TPACK, a moderate effect for AISE, a smaller effect for AIUI, and a negligible effect for AID. Games-Howell comparisons further showed that participants from Natural Sciences consistently scored highest on AI-TPACK, AISE, and AIUI. For AI-TPACK, the ordering was Natural Sciences \> Social Sciences \> Education \> Arts. For AISE, Natural Sciences scored signifi- cantly higher than all other groups, while Social Sciences also exceeded Education and Arts, with no signifi- cant difference between Education and Arts. For AIUI, Natural Sciences scored significantly higher than the

## 5. Discussion 

This study examined the psychological mechanisms through which AI-TPACK is associated with university teachers’ AI use intention in education, with a focus on the mediating role of AI self-efficacy and the moder- ating role of AI dependence. In addition, the study explored disciplinary differences among these variables. The findings provide empirically grounded insights into how AI-TPACK is translated into AI use intention in education, under what conditions this process is strengthened or weakened, and how disciplinary context shapes teachers’ AI-related profiles. 

First, the results confirmed that AI-TPACK was significantly and positively associated with AI use intention in education. This finding extends prior research (Ma & Lei, 2024; Sun et al., 2024) by demonstrating that this knowledge-intention link holds not only for pre-service teachers, but also for in-service university teachers using generative AI. The moderate effect (_β_ = .39) aligns with broader technology adoption research, which consistently shows that domain-specific knowledge strongly predicts teachers’ intentions to use new tools (Scherer et al., 2019; Tondeur et al., 2017). As generative AI tools are novel and complex, they place high cognitive and pedagogical demands on teachers. Therefore, AI-TPACK is important because it enables teach- ers to connect AI affordances with pedagogical purposes and disciplinary teaching needs, rather than treating AI as a standalone technical tool (Holmes et al., 2019; Luckin & Holmes, 2016). However, AI-TPACK alone does not fully explain AI use intention. Once AI self-efficacy was introduced, the direct effect of AI- TPACK was reduced. This partial effect supports Ertmer and Ottenbreit-Leftwich’s ([2010)](#orcid) argument that teacher knowledge and confidence are distinct internal variables that uniquely intersect to drive technology integration. It highlights that motivational factors are necessary to translate knowledge into teaching prac- tice. 

Second, AI self-efficacy mediated the relationship between AI-TPACK and AI use intention. The indirect effect accounted for about 29.60% of the total effect, indicating that AI self-efficacy is an important mecha- nism linking knowledge to intention. The two constituent paths were similar in size, with AI-TPACK signifi- cantly predicting AI self-efficacy (_β_ = .40) and AI self-efficacy significantly predicting AI use intention (_β_ = . 29). This suggests that the confidence-building process is a meaningful pathway rather than a minor one. This result is consistent with previous studies in educational technology, which have shown that self-efficacy can explain an important part of the relationship between knowledge and behavioral intention (Compeau & Higgins, [1995;](#orcid) Joo et al., 2018). At the same time, the mediation was partial. Even after AI self-efficacy was included, AI-TPACK still had a significant direct effect on AI use intention (_β_ = .27). This suggests that inte- grated AI knowledge may influence teachers’ intention through other pathways beyond confidence alone. For example, teachers with stronger AI-TPACK may also be more likely to recognize the instructional value and practical usefulness of generative AI, which are both closely related to technology adoption in the TAM literature (Davis, [1989;](#orcid) Venkatesh et al., 2003). In addition, previous studies have mainly treated AI self- efficacy either as an outcome of AI-related training (Maheshwari, 2024) or as an independent predictor of AI engagement (Y. Y. Wang & Chuang, 2024). The present study extends this line of research by testing AI self- efficacy as a mediator within the full knowledge-confidence-intention pathway in the context of generative AI. The reverse mediation test produced a slightly smaller indirect effect, which provides limited support for the proposed direction. However, as the data were cross-sectional, the causal order of the variables should still be interpreted with caution (Maxwell & Cole, 2007). 

Third, AI dependence moderated both the path from AI-TPACK to AI self-efficacy and the direct path from AI-TPACK to AI use intention. The indirect effect through AI self-efficacy was weaker at higher levels of AI dependence. The simple slope results are especially meaningful. The positive effect of AI-TPACK on AI self- efficacy decreased from 0.421 at low dependence to 0.259 at high dependence, although it remained significant at all three levels. This indicates that AI dependence does not fully eliminate the positive role of AI- TPACK, but is associated with a weaker relationship. This pattern is consistent with the cognitive offloading 

14 H. WU ET AL. 

literature, which suggests that excessive reliance on external tools can gradually reduce internal cognitive capability rather than simply support it (Chubb et al., [2022;](#orcid) Risko & Gilbert, 2016). Meanwhile, AI dependence also showed a significant positive direct association with AI use intention (_b_ = 0.15, _p_ = .002). Although this may seem counterintuitive, it suggests that some teachers may continue to report strong intentions to use AI not because of competence-based confidence, but because of habitual reliance. This interpretation is in line with dual-process views of technology use, which propose that behavioral intention can be shaped by both reflective and habitual processes at the same time (Söllner et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025). Taken together, these findings suggest that there are two different routes to AI use intention. One is a competence-driven route, which is based on professional knowledge and genuine confidence. The other is a dependency-driven route, which may be shaped by repeated reliance on AI. Although the competence-driven route appears more adaptive for teaching, its positive association with AI use intention becomes weaker as dependence rises. By contrast, the dependency-driven route may sustain reported AI use intention even when teachers’ self-efficacy is lower. This distinction is crucial for educational research. It demonstrates that high AI use inten- tion does not necessarily indicate pedagogical mastery, as the underlying motivational foundations differ fundamentally based on a teacher’s degree of AI dependence. 

Finally, the results revealed significant disciplinary differences in AI-TPACK, AI self-efficacy, and AI use intention, but not in AI dependence. Natural Sciences teachers scored highest on all three significant vari- ables, followed by Social Sciences, Education, and Arts. The effect size was strongest for AI-TPACK (ηp2 = . 162), moderate for AI self-efficacy (ηp2 = .101), and smaller for AI use intention (ηp2 = .045). This pattern sug- gests that disciplinary background shapes teachers’ AI-related knowledge more directly than it shapes their confidence or intention to use AI. This is consistent with previous research showing that teachers in some fields, especially those with greater exposure to computational tools and data-based work, are more likely to develop integrated AI knowledge (Kim et al., 2021; Starkey et al., 2023). The smaller disciplinary effect on AI use intention may indicate that intention is influenced not only by competence, but also by broader institu- tional and professional expectations. In other words, teachers across disciplines may increasingly view AI use as something professionally expected, even when their actual knowledge level differs. This interpretation is consistent with UTAUT research, which highlights the role of subjective norms in shaping technology use intention (Teo, 2011; Venkatesh et al., 2003). By contrast, no significant disciplinary difference was found in AI dependence. This result is important because it suggests that excessive reliance on AI is not limited to partic- ular academic fields or technical backgrounds. Instead, AI dependence may be better understood as a more general psychological and behavioral tendency, shaped by individual coping habits and patterns of reliance rather than by disciplinary context alone (Y. Du et al., [2026;](#orcid) Wu et al., 2025). The stability of AI dependence across disciplines supports treating it as a domain-general boundary condition, and further distinguishes it from AI-related competence constructs, which are clearly more discipline-sensitive. 

## 6. Theoretical and practical implications 

Theoretically, this study makes several contributions to the literature on AI integration in higher education, particularly in relation to university teachers’ AI adoption in contexts where institutions increasingly expect AI-supported instruction. First, it extends the AI-TPACK framework by situating it within an SCT-informed pro- cess model, demonstrating that AI-related professional knowledge is associated with AI use intention both directly and indirectly through AI self-efficacy. This finding addresses an underexplored gap in the literature, where AI-TPACK has been predominantly conceptualized as a descriptive competence framework rather than a dynamic predictor of instructional behavior. By establishing AI self-efficacy as a theoretically grounded mediating mechanism, the present study provides a more complete account of how professional knowledge is converted into behavioral intentions in the generative AI context. Second, the study con- tributes to the growing literature on AI dependence by demonstrating its moderating role within a knowledge-efficacy-intention chain. The finding that AI dependence reduces the positive effect of AI-TPACK on both AI self-efficacy and AI use intention refines the theoretical understanding of how over-reliance on AI tools introduces a boundary condition in the SCT-based framework. Importantly, this finding suggests that SCT-based models of technology integration should not assume a uniformly positive knowledge-to- behavior pathway, but should account for the possibility that behavioral patterns of reliance may disrupt the 

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 15 

productive translation of professional knowledge. Third, the disciplinary difference findings contribute to a more contextualized understanding of AI integration in higher education, demonstrating that discipline constitutes a meaningful source of variation in teachers’ AI-related competence and intentions while leaving AI dependence largely unaffected. This distinction is theoretically important because it suggests that AI- related competence and AI dependence should not be interpreted as the same type of adoption outcome. This pattern implies that discipline-sensitive explanatory models may be more appropriate than universal frameworks for capturing AI adoption dynamics across academic communities. 

Practically, the findings carry several implications for faculty development policy and institutional strategy in Chinese higher education. For Chinese universities seeking to translate AI policy goals into classroom practice, the results suggest that faculty development should address not only teachers’ AI knowledge, but also their confidence, disciplinary needs, and reliance patterns. First, the significant and positive association between AI-TPACK and AI use intention, mediated by AI self-efficacy, suggests that professional develop- ment programs should prioritize integrated knowledge development rather than isolated technical training. Programs that support teachers in connecting AI capabilities with their specific pedagogical strategies and disciplinary content are more likely to generate the competence beliefs that translate into instructional adoption. Workshops, peer coaching models, and communities of practice that situate AI learning within authentic disciplinary contexts may be particularly effective in this regard. Such programs should use discipline-specific teaching cases and assessment tasks rather than relying mainly on generic demonstra- tions of AI tools. Second, the mediating role of AI self-efficacy shows that confidence-building should be treated as a distinct goal in training design. Programs that include gradual mastery experiences, opportuni- ties for reflective practice, and timely feedback may be more effective than approaches that focus only on knowledge delivery. In particular, low-stakes environments in which teachers can experiment with AI tools in relation to their own teaching tasks may provide a stronger basis for developing AI self-efficacy. Third, the moderating role of AI dependence highlights a potential risk in faculty development. Increasing teachers’ exposure to AI without encouraging reflective use may strengthen dependence rather than competence. Institutions should therefore include digital wellness and reflective use strategies in AI literacy programs, so that teachers become more aware of their reliance patterns and maintain autonomous professional judg- ment while using AI. Finally, the disciplinary difference findings suggest that faculty development interven- tions should be differentiated by disciplinary context. Given that Natural Sciences teachers already exhibit relatively stronger AI-related competence and intentions, support resources may be more urgently needed in the social sciences, education, and arts, where concerns about creativity, authenticity, and disciplinary identity may create distinctive barriers to AI adoption. Tailored programs that engage directly with these domain-specific tensions, rather than offering uniform technical training, are likely to be more effective in these contexts. 

## 7. Conclusion 

This study examined the relationships among AI-TPACK, AI self-efficacy, AI use intention, and AI dependence among university teachers in southwestern China. Grounded in SCT and the AI-TPACK framework, the study tested a moderated mediation model using a stratified random sample of 407 teachers. The results showed that AI-TPACK was significantly and positively associated with AI use intention in education, and that this relationship was partially mediated by AI self-efficacy. AI dependence moderated both the direct and indi- rect paths between AI-TPACK and AI use intention. Significant disciplinary differences were also found, with Natural Sciences teachers scoring highest on AI-TPACK, AI self-efficacy, and AI use intention. By contrast, AI dependence remained stable across disciplines. Collectively, these findings deepen understanding of the psychological process through which AI-related professional knowledge is translated into instructional intention, clarify the boundary role of AI dependence, and provide evidence that AI adoption in higher education is shaped by disciplinary factors. 

Several limitations should be noted. First, the cross-sectional design does not allow causal conclusions. The mediation and moderated mediation findings should therefore be interpreted as statistical relationships that are consistent with the proposed model and the current research setting, rather than as proof of causal mechanisms. Future research employing longitudinal or intervention-based designs would provide stronger 

16 H. WU ET AL. 

evidence of directionality. Second, the sample came from a single normal university in southwestern China, which limits the generalizability of the findings. Future research should test the model across different insti- tution types, regions, and national settings. Third, all variables were measured through self-report, which may introduce social desirability and response consistency bias. In addition, participants’ prior awareness of the general research purpose may have increased socially desirable responding or encouraged responses aligned with perceived institutional expectations regarding AI integration. Future studies should include more objective indicators, such as AI usage logs or performance-based measures, to better capture actual adoption behavior. They may also use more neutral study descriptions and balanced item wording while still preserving adequate informed consent. Finally, both Harman’s single-factor test and the CLF approach indi- cated that the present model was unlikely to be substantially influenced by common method bias. Neverthe- less, these procedures remain limited in single-source cross-sectional research. Future studies adopting multi-source and multi-method designs would help further strengthen the validity of the results. 

Despite these limitations, this study provides theoretically grounded and empirically supported evidence that AI self-efficacy functions as a key psychological mechanism linking AI-TPACK to AI use intention, while AI dependence constrains the productive operation of this pathway, offering a refined conceptual map for understanding and promoting university teachers’ adaptive engagement with generative AI in education.
